metadata.title: Oracle Stock Drops While $40 Billion Funding Need Looms

content.text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), the enterprise-software giant going all-in on cloud infrastructure, disclosed plans to raise roughly $40 billion in fiscal 2027 as its shares fell about 1.7% Friday morning. That is a monster funding requirement. Half could come from Oracle's already announced $20 billion at-the-market equity program, while management does not expect to issue more debt during calendar 2026. The message is simple: Oracle sees huge cloud demand coming, but getting the capacity online is going to cost serious money.
And the demand is huge. Remaining performance obligations rocketed 363% year over year to $638 billion, with another $85 billion piling on in just one quarter. That backlog gives Oracle extraordinary revenue visibility. It also creates an extraordinary infrastructure bill. Operating cash flow jumped 54% to $32 billion in fiscal 2026, yet free cash flow still crashed to negative $23.7 billion as spending exploded. Oracle already raised $43 billion through debt and another $5 billion through equity during the year. This is the trade-off investors cannot ignore: the AI cloud opportunity is getting bigger, but so is the check Oracle has to write to capture it.
That makes the stock's valuation particularly interesting. Oracle closed at $153.14 on August 14 versus a GF Value estimate of $190.69, putting the shares 19.69% below GF Value. The market is offering a discount, but it is not giving Oracle a free pass. Planned fiscal 2027 funding is roughly 125% of its latest annual operating cash flow. If that $638 billion backlog converts into high-margin cloud revenue, today's spending binge could look like the price Oracle paid to become an AI infrastructure heavyweight. If cash burn stays brutal while equity issuance climbs, shareholders could feel the pain first. The next battle is no longer about whether Oracle has demand. It is about whether Oracle can turn that demand into cash faster than it burns cash building for it.
